articles.text: Piedmont’s urban forest is facing serious challenges with rising temperatures globally due to climate change. Nancy Kent, Piedmont’s Parks & Projects manager, spoke with the Post to discuss why Piedmont’s trees are dying and what the city plans to do. As summer heat continues to increase, trees planted 40 to 50 years ago are not well-equipped to deal with this changing climate. Piedmont’s Dracena Park has lost more than 50 trees due to increasing temperatures and less rainfall. “A lot of the conifers are the ones that we’ve seen die out,” said Kent. “These were all trees that were planted 50 years ago, and their natural range was probably colder than Piedmont. They can no longer survive in the current landscape they’re in because it’s just hotter and drier, and the rain is coming at different times or infrequently.” The tree most heavily impacted is the California coast live oak (Quercus agrifolia). It’s Piedmont’s third most abundant tree in the canopy and arborists believe that this oak may struggle as the climate continues to warm. In response, the city is actively planting trees that are more adaptive to the changing climate. According to Kent, this is new territory for the city, which has the challenge of projecting 50 years down the line that the trees they plant now will still be healthy. articles.text: On Thursday, April 2, at around 1:45 a.m., a magnitude 4.6 earthquake shook Bay Area residents out of their sleep. The earthquake originated near Boulder Creek, an unincorporated area in the Santa Cruz Mountains. Over 27,000 people in the region reported feeling the temblor, including in areas far from the epicenter like Sacramento and Santa Rosa, according to the USGS. The Bay Area remains at high risk of a damaging earthquake, according to the USGS, which estimates a 72% chance of a 6.7 magnitude or higher. An earthquake this large would cause a lot of damage to very populated areas. The best way to protect yourself and others in case of an emergency is to prepare for the worst and hope for the best. Piedmont’s Fire Department has shared tips on what residents should prepare in case of a large, damaging earthquake. Step one is to create a household emergency communication plan. In this plan, the department recommends that residents identify an out-of-area contact who lives outside the Bay Area to act as a central information source. articles.text: A week later his disciples were again in the house, and Thomas was with them. Although the doors were shut, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” — John 20:26 The Vanderbilt Divinity Library Revised Common Lectionary website suggests this prayer for the week after Easter. I trust that it speaks to you as it does to me. O God, your Son remained with his disciples after his resurrection, teaching them to love all people as neighbors. As his disciples in this age, we offer our prayers on behalf of the universe in which we are privileged to live and our neighbors with whom we share it. The current NASA Artemis II moon flight reminds that we are part of local communities as well as part of a universe that stretches to infinity. As such, Jesus’ words to his disciples as they hid behind closed doors in the days after that first Easter, “Peace be with you,” urge us to open our eyes and our hearts and see that while we are tempted to concern ourselves only with our own survival, we are responsible to care for the seas, the skies and stars. Our call is to seek the well-being of strangers, sojourners, seers and seekers in all times and all places. Jesus’ invitation to his disciples then and now, is to think large rather than to live small. I can’t help but believe that the Jesus who emerged from the tomb to say “Peace be with you,” would be well pleased with the words of astronaut Christina Koch, after the crew of Artemis II got back in touch with mission control after traveling past the dark side of the moon. Speaking to the people of Earth, Ms. Koch described a future when people will regularly go to the moon: “We will explore. We will build. We will build ships. We will visit again. We will construct science outposts. We will drive rovers. We will do radio astronomy. We will found companies. We will bolster industry.” But she ended by saying “We will inspire but ultimately, we will always choose Earth. We will always choose each other.” Peace be with you. Choose Earth. Choose each other. Pray for the well-being of the universe. Friends, join with me in believing that Easter has implications of cosmic proportion. Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland and currently Interim Pastor at Shell Ridge Community Church in Walnut Creek.
articles.title: After Easter

But above all, the teachers and staff are exceptional — dedicated professionals who know our kids by name and push them to grow. Jill attended Piedmont schools herself and had the same experience. Measure H renews the existing parcel tax that funds over $12 million — more than 20% of the PUSD budget. This is not a tax increase. It’s a continuation of nearly 40 years of community commitment. If Measure H fails, the district would be forced to cut $12 million annually, leading to devastating teacher layoffs and gutted programs. Whether or not you have children in our schools, Measure H protects what makes Piedmont, Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont Gas & Auto Repair, located at 340 Highland Ave, reopened after a lengthy closure to satisfy new California laws. The station took down its fences late last week and is actively serving gas to drivers. The station was closed under a state mandate that took effect on January 1. A California law effective September 25, 2014, changed the underground storage tank (UST) program regarding design and construction. The law states that a single-walled storage tank must have secondary containment and a continuous leak detection system If not stations were to be closed by December 31, 2025. Single-walled storage tanks increase the risk of leaking due to rust and corrosion. The law is intended to prevent hazardous substances from polluting soil, groundwater, streams, and other sources of drinking water. If the station had not complied it would have faced serious fines of $500 to $5,000 per day per underground storage tank according to the State Resources Control Board. The station could also have been be red-tagged by the Unified Program Agency, which could prevent fuel deliveries and dispensing. Piedmont Gas & Auto Repair has spent the last three months removing its single-walled underground storage tank and replacing it with an underground tank that complies with the secondary containment and leak detection system requirements. articles.text: Hamlet is an AI-powered civic technology platform that makes local government meetings searchable and accessible. Sunil Rajaraman, the CEO and founder of Hamlet, became passionate about local government when he decided to run for the Orinda, CA City Council. He wanted to get more involved in the community, and by attending local council meetings, he noticed a significant barrier to entry for those interested in local government. “As an average resident, it’s impossible to understand what’s happening unless you attend regularly or read the transcripts. It’s a huge time commitment,” said Rajaraman. He identified that the barrier to entry for local government was so time-consuming. Most people are unable to focus on their local government’s decisions, which impact our day-to-day lives the most. “I think that the problem is that you know most people are focused on federal-level politics,” he stated. “The stuff that affects our day-to-day lives that flies under the radar is local politics. And while it’s great, we have a lot of people engaged at the federal and state level, but council chambers are empty.” Rajaraman would use AI to simplify council meetings and get up to speed on hot topic issues. Through his use of AI, he was inspired to create a platform that could help local communities easily digest their local governments’ meetings. “Everybody should have access to as much of that raw information as possible,” he continued. “I think that’ll make American communities better if people actually understand what’s happening in their city councils and planning commissions.” Through this, Rajarman founded Hamlet, his AI company designed to make local meets more accessible. Hamlet indexes thousands of government meeting transcripts from city councils, planning commissions, zoning boards, and other public bodies across the United States. They then make this information searchable by using a combination of official transcripts, video recordings, and AI-powered transcription. “I want people to be engaged so we can put better people into office in certain cities and make sure people are informed about how the decision-making and democratic process works at the local level,” said Rajaraman. Rajaraman’s company uses Hamlet to create city deep dives on their platform, The District. The District is a data-driven deep dive into local cities, highlighting the biggest topics and data about who has spoken the most at council meetings or the most repeated topics. To avoid potential biases, the company writes about cities Sunil Rajaraman, CEO & founder of Hamlet AI with no financial ties to the company. Readers can follow this link to read about Piedmont’s deep dive: https://district.myhamlet. com/articles/piedmonts-deliberation. The next steps for Hamlet are to continue expanding and improving their coverage of local government. “We’re adding more and more cities to our database, and we want to build the most important company focused on local government,” Rajaraman said. “We should understand how local government makes decisions. And within that, residents should understand it transparently.” To learn more about Hamlet and look at Piedmont’s council meetings broken down, you can find them at the following link: https://www.myhamlet.com/
articles.title: Hamlet AI revolutionizes nationwide local government public meeting coverage

articles.text: When people talk about “finding your people,” the advice is usually some version of: join something. Join a book club. Take a class in something you are interested in. Find a group to volunteer with on a topic that you are passionate about. And that is not actually bad advice, but it is incomplete. Because finding your people is not only about where you go a few times. It’s about what happens next. There’s a study from the University of Kansas that looks at how long it takes to form friendships. The numbers are surprisingly high. It takes about 40 to 60 hours to become a casual friend, 80 to 100 hours to become a friend, and around 200 hours to become a close friend. Which means most friendships don’t fail because we chose the wrong activity group. They stall out somewhere around hour two. Does this sound familiar to you? You have a good first conversation and discover you both like the same podcast, or the same kind of music, or the same way of spending a Saturday morning. And then… nothing really happens after that. The connection stays theoretical. So I’ve been thinking about that first step differently. Yes, shared interests matter. They make it easier to start. A book group, a ski club, a random conversation about something you both enjoy. That’s often where it begins. But that’s not where friendship is built. At some point, someone has to do the slightly uncomfortable thing of continuing it. Asking, “Do you want to grab a coffee sometime?” or suggesting a walk or a hike. You’ve got to follow up instead of assuming it will happen naturally because it won’t! And then doing it again… and again. Those first 39 hours will likely feel awkward and a little uneven because you are still figuring each other out. The conversation won’t always flow and you might feel like you are oversharing or not sharing enough. It can seem easier to retreat back to surface-level interactions or to keep things contained within the original context, but this is the part that actually builds towards something. Finding common ground is not just about discovering one thing you both like. It is about slowly learning each other’s lives. The parts that overlap and the parts that don’t. What matters to the other person. What they are carrying. What they are excited about. That kind of connection does not happen quickly. It takes time, and it takes some willingness to stay in the awkward middle where nothing is fully formed yet. So here is a small experiment. Connection Experiment: Finding your people By Nina Meehan When people talk about “finding your people,” the advice is usually some version of: join something. Join a book club. Take a class in something you are interested in. Find a group to volunteer with on a topic that you are passionate about. And that is not actually bad advice, but it is incomplete. Because finding your people is not only about where you go a few times. It’s about what happens next. There’s a study from the University of Kansas that looks at how long it takes to form friendships. The numbers are surprisingly high. It takes about 40 to 60 hours to become a casual friend, 80 to 100 hours to become a friend, and around 200 hours to become a close friend. Which means most friendships don’t fail because we chose the wrong activity group. They stall out somewhere around hour two. Does this sound familiar to you? You have a good first conversation and discover you both like the same podcast, or the same kind of music, or the same way of spending a Saturday morning. And then… nothing really happens after that. The connection stays theoretical. So I’ve been thinking about that first step differently. Yes, shared interests matter. They make it easier to start. A book group, a ski club, a random conversation about something you both enjoy. That’s often where it begins. But that’s not where friendship is built. At some point, someone has to do the slightly uncomfortable thing of continuing it. Asking, “Do you want to grab a coffee sometime?” or suggesting a walk or a hike. You’ve got to follow up instead of assuming it will happen naturally because it won’t! And then doing it again… and again. Those first 39 hours will likely feel awkward and a little uneven because you are still figuring each other out. The conversation won’t always flow and you might feel like you are oversharing or not sharing enough. It can seem easier to retreat back to surface-level interactions or to keep things contained within the original context, but this is the part that actually builds towards something. Finding common ground is not just about discovering one thing you both like. It is about slowly learning each other’s lives. The parts that overlap and the parts that don’t. What matters to the other person. What they are carrying. What they are excited about. That kind of connection does not happen quickly. It takes time, and it takes some willingness to stay in the awkward middle where nothing is fully formed yet. So here is a small experiment. The next time you have a conversation with someone where there is even a hint of shared interest, do one more thing. Make one specific invitation. Not “we should do this sometime,” but something real with a time, a place and a simple plan. And then follow through. You do not need to join whole new group and you do not need a perfect alignment of interests. You just need one interaction, and then another, and then enough time for something real to start to take shape. articles.text: On the weekend of March 14, the Highlander Robotics team traveled to San Francisco with their new robot “Wisp” for the FIRST Robotics Competition’s San Francisco District Event at St. Ignatius High School. There they won the FIRST Impact Award and qualified for the NorCal District Championship in April. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January, played by two alliances of three robots in an arena roughly the size of a basketball court. Roughly 3500 teams of 9th to 12th graders construct an entirely new robot each season and competitions begin eight weeks after kickoff. In this year’s game called Rebuilt, robots shoot 6-inch foam balls into an 8-foot high funnel while crossing field obstacles and climbing rungs of a ladder before time runs out. At their first competition of the season, the Highlanders finished qualification rounds ranked 5th of 38 teams with an 8-4 record. During alliance selection they were chosen as the second pick of the draft by Alliance 2, captained by the Aragon Robotics Team from San Mateo. In the opening round of the double-elimination playoffs they defeated Alliance 7, Deus Ex Machina, the SOTA Cyberdragons, and Bay Robotics. In the second round they fell to the third-seeded OtterBots alliance and dropped to the lower bracket, where they were eliminated in Round 4 by the 4th seed Pit member Sattvik Sapuram works to maintain Wisp between rounds. The team has 62 students from 12 local high schools. Drive team members Sam Charlson (left), Mason Kim, Cassie Colby, and Max Seiden prepare strategy before their match. Alliance and finished 4th overall. In the awards ceremony the Highlanders were awarded FIRST’s most prestigious award, the Impact Award, which honors the team that best represents a model for other teams to emulate and embodies the mission of FIRST. Judges cited the opening of a multi-level robotics practice space partnership with Piedmont Makers, the adoption of the scouting software that the Highlanders publish each year by over 800 teams, and the team’s open source software training curriculum as reasons they were deserving of the award. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team wrapped up a busy week, competing in three events in just four days. The Highlanders sent six athletes to the prestigious Stanford Invitational in Palo Alto on Friday and Saturday, April 3-4, and sent two to the Dave Shimansky Pole Vault Invitational on April 4 at San Ramon Valley HS in Danville. Both the boys and girls teams won a Western Alameda County Conference meet with Alameda on Wednesday, April 1 at Burrell Field in San Leandro. At the Stanford Invitational, Piedmont notably qualified its 4x400 relay team and Sebastien Swain in the 800 to the famous Arcadia Invitational on Friday and Saturday, April 10-11. It is considered the marquee event throughout the year for track and field. Swain will also run alongside Rehan Mumtaz, Marius Arno, and Maddox Ma in the 4 x 400 relay. “The Arcadia Invitational is the #1 high school track and field event in the world. Over 200 athletes that competed at Arcadia went on to compete in the Olympics, like Noah Lyles who holds the boys all-time 100 meter record, Marion Jones who holds the girls all-time 200m record, and Sydney McLaughlin who holds the girls all-time 300 hurdles record. This year the fun name is Quincy Wilson, who as a 16 year old received a gold medal as a member of the Team USA 4x400m team. Somehow our little public school has sent at least one athlete to Arcadia every year since 2021,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. Swain finished 12th of 18 in the 800 at the Stanford Invitational, in a fast time of 1:56.21. It marked just his sixth event since returning from knee surgery. “We’re trying to not get too excited but it sure seems like Seb’s just a few steps away from being fully back. For me, it’s less about his time and more about how he ran those two races. He was confident and aggressive,” Assadi said. In the 4x400, Mumtaz, Swain, Arno, and Ma finished 13th of 23 teams with a time of 3:27.21. They were the second fastest team from the North Coast Section behind Windsor, which placed ninth. “I’m pumped about how the boys ran that 4x4,” said Assadi. “Seb was the key as he moved us from fifth to second. Maddox took us home and showed us why he was a no brainer decision to anchor,” Mumtaz and Ma also ran in the 4x100, while Diego Hurwitz and Jason Shum replaced Swain and Arno. They finished 22nd in 43.79. Dave Shimansky Pole Vault Invitational results Avedis Gourjian finished the boys’ event sixth of 24 athletes with a height of 11 feet, 6 inches. We have a lot of sophomores and want that upward trajectory. We played some really tough teams at the start of the season, and that’s going to make us better in the long run,” said coach Eric Olson. articles.text: Staff Photos Dahlia Osman scored three goals against San Rafael, the first hat trick of her lacrosse career. Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team won a 6-5 battle against San Rafael on Thursday, April 1 at Witter Field. They have four matches left in the regular season. It’s been a matter of persevering through injuries for Piedmont this season. “I feel like we are the (Golden State) Warriors. It’s like every game we are without someone. I’ve never had a team where we were without so many bodies. But they are figuring it out, they are getting better every day. That’s all we care about,” said coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont has a young squad, including freshman Sydney Latvala as a key player. She scored twice and had an assist against San Rafael. The Highlanders currently the No. 25 ranked school in North Coast Section by MaxPreps.com, which will put them on pace for a No. 9 seed in the Division 2 bracket. “It’s all about effort. Everyone is trying hard and putting 100 percent into everything. The ground balls really matter and we’re focusing on improving on that. I feel like we’re making stronger connections on attack and stay calm,” Latvala said. 6-5 win over San Rafael Both teams were tied 2-2 through the first quarter. The the Highlanders’ defense holding the Bulldogs without a goal in the second quarter, while scoring one of their own to take a 3-2 lead into halftime. Piedmont scored once in the third quarter while conceding two, making it 4-4 going into the final going. San Rafael scored the first goal in the fourth quarter, but PHS roared back with the final two goals of the game. In the first quarter, San Rafael struck first at the 7:39 mark. Piedmont won the ensuing faceoff, scoring just 33 seconds later when Elliott Hondorp sent in a shot. articles.text: Piedmont’s Competition Pool After a lengthy construction process and significant delays, Piedmont’s community pool is opening this weekend on Saturday, April 11. Many residents are excited to jump into the new pool, but none moreso than Piedmont High School boys water polo coach, Rik Krumins. Krumins has coached at PHS for the past 10 years alongside John Savage in both an assistant and head coaching role. This past year, Krumins and Savage led the team to a 16-9 record and an 8-1 record in the West Alameda County League. In the wait for a new pool, both the girls’ and boys’ water polo teams have struggled to find a continuous place to practice. As construction for the pool began, the team trained in North Berkeley (King Pool), then over the course of time, they’ve been training and competing at Berkeley High School, Mills College, Laney College, Chabot College (Hayward), and Campolindo HS in Moraga. “This has been the biggest challenge for both the girls and boys teams in retaining athletes for the program over the course of the construction,” said Krumins. “I have been lucky enough that the water polo athletes have amazing parents and support groups who have been willing to commute to these facilities over the past 5-6 years, but we have taken a hit.” Now that the pool is open, the ease of access for student athletes and teams to practice will help the program tremendously. “This is a game-changer for the student-athletes as well. The ability to walk across campus to compete in front of their own student body will bring immense joy to these athletes. Something our water polo and aquatics programs have missed since the pool closed,” Krumins said. Krumins has had the opportunity to walk through the facility and has peered over the fence “thousands of times.” The competition pool will be where the sports teams will stake their presence, and Krumins is satisfied with its dimensions and adaptability. “Piedmont HS students will be training and competing in a proper ‘world aquatic’ (Olympic, Collegiate, High School) sized facility,” Krumins continued about the opportunity for youth programs. “The flexibility with nets and pool design allows the Piedmont Recreation Department, in partnership with me, to run youth water polo clinics and junior programs. Here is an opportunity to offer this for our youth, and I plan on doing this.” The coaching staff submitted the 2026 training and competition schedule last week for the desired pool times. The team has not yet been provided the schedule, but they’re anticipating it will be published soon. Its season starts in the fall. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School girls softball team notched its first win of the season in dominant fashion on Monday, March 30, at Witter Field, beating El Cerrito’s Korematsu Middle School 10-0 in four innings. The Scots are led by a talented core of 8th graders who set the tone on both offense and defense. Bailey Gregovich and Madi Farboud both pitched nearly flawlessly in the shutout, striking out 6 while yielding only 4 hits and not walking a batter. Catcher Simone Tornatore went the distance behind, not allowing a single passed ball and making a key tag at the plate to stop a run. Defensive gems also came from 6th grader Keira Spina, who made a sensational catch at shortstop with the bases loaded in the first inning that deflated Korematsu’s early surge, and from 7th grader Mackenzie Ewen who snared a sharp liner to left in the third inning. Middle school softball is a relatively new sport to Piedmont since last year with many players having played in recreational softball and baseball through Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation. The team made it to the middle school championship last year where it lost to Berkeley’s Willard Middle School. This season, Piedmont Middle School is scheduled to play Albany, Berkeley’s King, Longfellow, and Willard, as well as schools in the Oakland Athletic League. pages.text: Wednesday, April 8, 2026 15 Piedmont water polo coach excited for the new pool Middle School softball team shuts out Korematsu in 4 innings The Piedmont Middle School girls softball team notched its first win of the season in dominant fashion on Monday, March 30, at Witter Field, beating El Cerrito’s Korematsu Middle School 10-0 in four innings. The Scots are led by a talented core of 8th graders who set the tone on both offense and defense. Bailey Gregovich and Madi Farboud both pitched nearly flawlessly in the shutout, striking out 6 while yielding only 4 hits and not walking a batter. Catcher Simone Tornatore went the distance behind, not allowing a single passed ball and making a key tag at the plate to stop a run. Defensive gems also came from 6th grader Keira Spina, who made a sensational catch at shortstop with the bases loaded in the first inning that deflated Korematsu’s early surge, and from 7th grader Mackenzie Ewen who snared a sharp liner to left in the third inning. The Scots offense was spurred by Farboud with three RBIs, Ewen with two RBIs, as well as a host of other contributors up and down the lineup. Spina, Clara Blanchard, Olive Dao-Hoang, Cate Penrod and Evie Joerger all drove in runs. Middle school softball is a relatively new sport to Piedmont since last year with many players having played in recreational softball and baseball through Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation. The team made it to the middle school championship last year where it lost to Berkeley’s Willard Middle School. This season, Piedmont Middle School is scheduled to play Albany, Berkeley’s King, Longfellow, and Willard, as well as schools in the Oakland Athletic League. Next up, the Scots will face off against Albany Middle School after Spring Break on Thursday, April 16, at 6 pm at Witter Softball Field. Piedmont’s Competition Pool By Jake Lannon After a lengthy construction process and significant delays, Piedmont’s community pool is opening this weekend on Saturday, April 11. Many residents are excited to jump into the new pool, but none moreso than Piedmont High School boys water polo coach, Rik Krumins. Krumins has coached at PHS for the past 10 years alongside John Savage in both an assistant and head coaching role. This past year, Krumins and Savage led the team to a 16-9 record and an 8-1 record in the West Alameda County League. In the wait for a new pool, both the girls’ and boys’ water polo teams have struggled to find a continuous place to practice. As construction for the pool began, the team trained in North Berkeley (King Pool), then over the course of time, they’ve been training and competing at Berkeley High School, Mills College, Laney College, Chabot College (Hayward), and Campolindo HS in Moraga. “This has been the biggest challenge for both the girls and boys teams in retaining athletes for the program over the course of the construction,” said Krumins. “I have been lucky enough that the water polo athletes have amazing parents and support groups who have been willing to commute to these facilities over the past 5-6 years, but we have taken a hit.” Now that the pool is open, the ease of access for student athletes and teams to practice will help the program tremendously. “This is a game-changer for the student-athletes as well. The ability to walk across campus to compete in front of their own student body will bring immense joy to these athletes. Something our water polo and aquatics programs have missed since the pool closed,” Krumins said. Krumins has had the opportunity to walk through the facility and has peered over the fence “thousands of times.” The competition pool will be where the sports teams will stake their presence, and Krumins is satisfied with its dimensions and adaptability. “Piedmont HS students will be training and competing in a proper ‘world aquatic’ (Olympic, Collegiate, High School) sized facility,” Krumins continued about the opportunity for youth programs. “The flexibility with nets and pool design allows the Piedmont Recreation Department, in partnership with me, to run youth water polo clinics and junior programs. Here is an opportunity to offer this for our youth, and I plan on doing this.” The coaching staff submitted the 2026 training and competition schedule last week for the desired pool times. The team has not yet been provided the schedule, but they’re anticipating it will be published soon. Its season starts in the fall. articles.text: Now Showing Through April Women in Focus by Denise Deleray is showing through April at Studios 11 at 560 Second Street in Oakland. The show is a compelling portrait exhibition exploring both the diversity and shared humanity of women across cultures. Featuring over a dozen works, the show presents faces from around the world— each portrait offering a unique story, while collectively revealing striking similarities in expression, presence, and identity. The exhibit also features an interactive portion of mixable miniature portraits. Denise Deleray, a San Francisco native, has been painting at Studios 11 for nearly a decade. She is especially drawn to portraying women as a way to raise awareness of important or under-recognized figures throughout history. The charming Studios 11 gallery sits just behind The Grand Gallery at the same address. While The Grand Gallery features over 30 local artists and has been operating for about two years, Studios 11 has a much longer history—serving as an independent creative space for over 15 years, evolving alongside a variety of neighboring front-facing galleries. • Gallery Hours: Saturday and Sunday 12 - 5 p.m. • Opening Reception: Saturday April 11, 2026, 1 - 4 p.m. For more information contact via email: Denisedeleray@mac. com.

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is hosting Art Bash, the museum’s signature annual fundraiser, on Wednesday, April 29. Art Bash raises more than $2.5 annually to benefit the museum’s education and family programs, as well as community engagement events that benefit over 150,000 people every year. The event transforms the museum’s entire campus into a multi-layered experience of art, performances and social activities. This year’s celebration also marks the 10th anniversary of SFMOMA’s building expansion. Art Bash 2026 begins with a ticketed dinner featuring a live auction of works by contemporary artists led by Phyllis Kao of Sotheby’s and a multisensory installation created by Jeffrey Gibson. After the dinner phase, the event broadens to a museum-wide party with immersive art installations by Bay Area artists Rose D’Amato and Rupy C. Tut. alongside “Zenni: The Art of Seeing,” an immersive photo experience for attendees. This year’s musical lineup, presented in partnership with Stern Grove Festival, features Shannon & The Clams, Ruby Ibarra and Wonway Posibul during the main party, while premium lounge performances will include Cruise Control and DJ heyLove. Tickets may be purchased at sfmoma.org/artbash. SFMOMA’s Art Bash returns this spring.

articles.text: The international photography exhibition Ocean Photographer of the Year will make its U.S. debut April 24 inside a historic World War II aircraft hangar at Alameda Point. The exhibition, presented by Oceanographic Magazine and Blancpain, will run for one month and feature a selection of winning and finalist images from the global Ocean Photographer of the Year competition. The show is hosted locally by West End Arts District in partnership with Bay Photo Lab. Now in its fifth year, the competition received more than 15,000 submissions from photographers worldwide. The exhibition includes images from categories such as wildlife, fine art, adventure, conservation, human connection, and young photographer of the year, along with the Female Fifty Fathoms Award recognizing women in ocean photography. “We’re thrilled to bring Ocean Photographer of the Year to Alameda Point and to invite the community to experience this powerful ode to the ocean in such a unique setting,” said Tara Pilbrow, Executive Director of West End Arts District. “By breathing new life into Alameda Point’s military history, we’re also expressing our commitment to the kind of future we want to see – one rooted in creativity, environmental awareness, and shared cultural experiences.” Alongside the international exhibition, visitors can explore “Bay Perspectives,” a gallery featuring ocean photography focused on the San Francisco Bay and the California coast. The space will also include interactive marine science exhibits presented by the Sailing Science Center. “The stories behind these photographs are as compelling as the visuals themselves – they challenge us to see the ocean not just as a place of wonder, but as a world in need of our care,” said Daryl Karp, director and chief executive officer of the Australian National Maritime Museum. Public hours are Saturdays and Sundays from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with additional programs scheduled on Thursdays and Fridays. An opening gala hosted by Bay Photo Lab will mark the company’s 50th anniversary. “Our mission is to share the ocean with non-ocean goers and photography is the most awesome conduit to do that,” said Will Harrison of Oceanographic Magazine. “Underwater photography is one of the most powerful allies in our fight to preserve and protect the ocean,” added Gaël Nicolle of Blancpain. For more information and to purchase tickets to the exhibition and events, visit www.westendartsdistrict.org.

articles.text: Production runs through April 16 at War Memorial Opera House The San Francisco Ballet performs August Bournonville’s La Sylphide at the War Memorial Opera House this Friday, April 10 to Thursday, April 16. La Sylphide follows James, a young Scotsman who becomes enchanted by a mysterious sylph on the day he is set to marry Effie. Drawn away from his wedding, James follows the sylph into the forest, leaving behind his fiancée and his former life. There, the witch Madge gives him a magical scarf, promising it will allow him to hold the sylph forever. Instead, when James places the scarf around her shoulders, the spell destroys her wings and causes her death. As James mourns, Effie marries Gurn, a rival who remained at her side. First staged in 1836, the ballet remains one of the defining works of the Romantic era, known for its light footwork and technique. Guests may enjoy live bagpipe music on the front steps of the Opera House from master bagpiper Fred Payne before each performance of La Sylphide. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet. org/productions/la-sylphide/. San Francisco Ballet’s past production of La Sylphide

articles.text: Shotgun Players’ 34th season opened with The Goat or, Who is Sylvia? by Edward Albee, playing at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through April 19. The Tony Award-winning play centers on Martin Gray, a successful architect whose personal life unravels after he tells his wife and son that he is in love with a goat named Sylvia. The disclosure leads to conflict within his family and raises questions about morality, loyalty and acceptance. The production is directed by Shotgun Players company member Kevin Clarke. In a statement, Clarke said the play “tests the limits of permissiveness” and asks audiences to consider the characters’ perspectives. William Giammona plays Martin Gray; Erin Mei Ling Stuart portrays his wife, Stevie Gray; Kevin Singer appears as Ross, a longtime family friend; and Joel Ochoa plays the couple’s son, Billy. The play premiered on Broadway in 2002 and won the Tony Award for best play. It was also named a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for drama in 2003. Perfor mances r un now through April 19. Showtimes are 7 p.m. Wednesdays and Thursdays, 8 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays and 2 p.m. on Sundays. A haptic tour and live audio-described performance will be offered April 12, with the tour at 1 p.m. and the performance at 2 p.m. Post-show discussions will follow Thursday and Sunday performances. articles.text: The Chicago-based ballet company returns to UC Berkeley this month. Cal Performances welcomes The Joffrey Ballet back to Zellerbach Hall for three performances of Midsummer Night’s Dream, marking the West Coast premiere of the work by Swedish choreographer Alexander Ekman. The Joffrey Ballet is based in Chicago and is known for blending classical ballet with contemporary work. The company has been the resident dance company at Lyric Opera House since the 2021–22 season and continues an eight-year residency partnership with Cal Performances that began in 2024. Ekman’s Midsummer Night’s Dream takes inspiration from Scandinavian midsummer traditions rather than William Shakespeare’s play of the same name. The production features nearly three dozen dancers, surreal stage design, and a live original score by Swedish composer Mikael Karlsson. Vocals will be performed by Anna von Hausswolff, whose music combines post-rock, minimalism, and pop influences. Photo courtesy of The Joffrey Ballet Additional musicians include percussionist Niklas Brommare and pianist Jorge Ivars, joined by a string quartet. The performances are scheduled for Friday, April 17, at 7 p.m.; Saturday, April 18, at 8 p.m.; and Sunday, April 19, at 3 p.m. The Friday performance will also serve as the centerpiece of Cal Performances at UC Berkeley’s 2026 gala. Tickets are available online at www.calperformances.org or by calling the box office at (510) 642-9988.

articles.text: The Quiet Girl has been referred to as a whisper of a film, and it is that and so much more. Based on the 2010 novella Foster by noted Irish author Claire Keegan, and the 2023 winner of the Oscar in the Best International Feature Film category. It is an unassuming, beautifully written coming-of-age drama about a nine-year-old girl named Cait (Catherine Clinch) whose silence has become her refuge. The film opens with Cait lying in a lush tall-grass farm field, hidden, looking up at a blue sky. A voice in the distance is calling her name. We soon discover that she lives with an impoverished farm family. To her shame, on occasion, Cait wets her bed, and is harshly ignored by both her parents (Kate Nic Chonaonaigh and Michael Patric) and many siblings. School is a struggle, some classmates cruel, and something to be endured, a place where she is often ignored or ridiculed. Cait’s father, Da, is shiftless, preferring to spend time in a local pub drinking his pint than preparing for the seasonal harvest. Finding it difficult to feed all the children (Cait’s mother, Mam, is once again pregnant), the parents decide to send Cait to spend the summer with a distant cousin, Eibhlin (Carey Crowley), and her husband Sean (Andrew Bennett), who are rural dairy farmers. Da drives her to the distant farm, saying little, and is so disengaged that when he leaves Cait with the the trunk of the car. And it’s with this couple (it takes Sean a bit longer than Eibhlin to warm up to the girl) she experiences a kindness and generosity of attention and concern that she has never known before. Cait comes to realize, slowly, tentatively, that there is a world, and a way of being in that world, which is far different from the one she has known growing up. Expecting indifference or cruelty she discovers the opposite, an unexpected loving embrace, and so her silence, her reflexive response to life, is slowly lifted Catherine Clinch and Carrie Crowley in The Quiet Girl couple, absent even a goodbye, he drives off with her suitcase still in and Cait, in effect, comes out of hiding and begins to blossom. The Quiet Girl is a beautiful film, gentle and moving, subtle yet deeply emotive. It is a narrative about the power of kindness that is all too often underrated if not absent; yet, when encountered, it can heal, even delight, and be transformative. As it does with Cait. The Quiet Girl. Written and directed by Colm Bairead. Starring Catherine Clinch, Carrie Crowley, Andrew Bennett. 1 hr., 34 min. PG-13. Released in 2022. Now streaming on Disney+/ Prime/HULU/Fandango/Apple tv.

articles.text: The Incredibles is an award winning, critically acclaimed animated action feature from Pixar – Walt Disney Studios to include a 77th Academy Awards Oscar (2005) and a Hugo Award, which was the first in the category of animated feature. It stars a family of under-theradar superheroes. The patriarch of the family is Mr. Incredible (Craig T. Nelson), a popular superhero, beloved for his dramatic rescues, foiled bank robberies, and super-powered interventions. But despite his passion for what he does, the public grows weary of the collateral damage that occurs with each rescue. As a result he and his new wife, Elastic Girl (Holly Hunter), are forced into what is called the Superhero Relocation Program, and required by the government to live normal lives, using the names Bob and Helen Parr. Now flash forward 15 years. Bob is an insurance salesman, and he and Helen have three children – Dash (Spencer Fox), Violet (Sarah Vowell), and baby Jack Jack. As it turns out, Bob is growing increasingly dissatisfied with his mundane life. He yearns for the good old days when he was Mr. Incredible, and reminisces each day on the way to work (stuck in traffic) with Lucius Best, Mr. Frozone (Samuel L. Jackson), while they listen to a police scanner, tempting both of them to help out. They know that they’ve got the right stuff. One day, a mysterious woman named Mirage (Elizabeth Pena) appears and makes them a job offer, and Bob seizes the opportunity to return to his role of Mr. Incredible. He is convinced that like those days of yesteryear, he can make a difference. He soon runs into an archenemy called Syndrome (Jason Lee), and it doesn’t take long before Mr. Incredible’s whole family is involved in running battles and action-oriented chases with this nemesis. The Incredibles is one of Pixar’s best, a wonderful example of high tech animation, lushly created backgrounds, slap-dash humor and jokes, with superhero costumes and signature masks. The kids will love it, as will the adults. The Incredibles. Directed and co-written by Brad Bird. Voiced by Craig T. Nelson, Holly Hunter, Samuel L. Jackson. articles.text: The Madison is a solid Paramount+ neo-western series set in Southwestern Montana along the Madison River. The first episode opens with two brothers, Preston Clyburn (Kurt Russell) and Paul Clyburn (Matthew Fox), fly-fishing on a wide, slow-moving river. Friendly banter passes between them as they trade suggestions about which fly is most likely to snag a good-size trout. Paul has long ago left his successful career for a life doing exactly what the two men are doing in that moment. In contrast, Preston and family – wife Stacy (Michelle Pfeiffer) and daughters plus children) live in New York City, all accustomed to an urban life style only affluence can offer. The Madison was was written by the talented and prolific Taylor Sheridan, whose western sagas debuted with the popular series Yellowstone and continued with the prequels 1883, and 1923. All three are exceptionally well-done productions and perfectly cast. Unexpectedly, the Clyburn family is swept up in a tragedy that rocks their world and asks them to examine what it means to confront an unexpected loss Michelle Pfeiffer and Kurt Russell in The Madison for which they feel completely unprepared. The Madison is just so good, and for those who enjoy this episodic tale, Paramount+ has announced that there will be a second season. articles.text: Hearing the news that Robert Redford, at the age of 89, had died caused me to pause and I felt a sense of disbelief. I suddenly realized that though I had seen recent photos of the actor, and watched The Old Man and the Gun (2018), purported to be his last film, I knew that decades had passed, evident in the deep lines in his face, in the almost casual and polite demeanor implicit in the narrative, the gun a mere prop. Was the film a metaphor, this smiling portrayal of an elderly bank robber who loves what he does – though on occasion he is caught and spends time in jail, he returns, not for the money but for the doing. Or is The Old Man and the Gun his very fond, even gentle way of saying farewell? I have since been struck by his timeless presence on the screen, something I had taken for granted, realizing now that he seemed to defy the gravity of aging. He would always be the all-American Hubbell Gardiner in the film The Way We Were (1973), or Sundance in the hugely popular Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969). His filmography is stunning, the variety and number of leading roles extensive. In recognition of his contribution to the film arts, the Academy presented him with an honorary award for his work as actor, director, narrator (voice over) and producer as well as the creation of the Sundance Festival in 1981, which annually has nurtured, screened and honrod the work of independent filmmakers. There isn’t space to list the many films in which he portrayed a leading character. His legacy, to include his efforts as an environmentalist, will ever be with us, and in the aggregate will remain an enduring tribute to his love of this larger than life art form and the power of film to tell a story. articles.text: A River Runs Through It, released in 1992, is a gently told period drama, beautifully photographed by Oscar-winning Philipe. Rousselot. It is set in Missoula, Montana, during a time that stretches from the end of WWI to the beginning of the Great Depression. The narrative, with voiceover by director Robert Redford, is based on the 1976 autobiography by Norman Maclean. The film follows the Maclean brothers, Norman (Craig Scheffer) and Paul (Brad Pitt), who as youngsters thrived in the bucolic surrounds of rural Missoula. They were taught the discipline, if not the art, of fly fishing on the nearby Blackfoot River by their Presbyterian minister father (Tom Skerritt) who gently merged religion with the early mornings the three spent standing in the rippling river, casting their lines out onto the eddying, rippling surface. Their time together, often spent sitting among the Ponderosa pines on the river banks, or finding a metronomic rhythm as they fished, moments when the morning light shimmered off the wet rocks, all of it a metaphor for their union, captured in the lyrical words of Maclean and spoken by Robert Redford. “In the slanting sun of the late afternoon the shadows of great branches reached from across the river, and the trees took the river in their arms. The shadows continued up the bank until they included us.” Regrettably, Norman Maclean passed away before the film was completed; however, his words frame a final, touching moment as Maclean, now nearing the end of his life, stands at the edge of the river, and with trembling hands slowly ties a fly to his line, and seemingly lost in the moment gazes off into the distance. “Eventually, all things merge into one, and the river runs through it. The river was cut by the world’s great flood and runs over rocks from the basement of time. On some of the rocks are timeless raindrops. Under the rocks are the words, and some of the words are theirs. I am haunted by waters.” A River Runs Through It. Directed by Robert Redford. Starring Brad Pitt, Craig Shaffer, Tom Skerritt. Voiceover by Robert Redford. 2 hrs., 3 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/Apple/Fandango/MGM+/Roku. Tom Skerritt, Craig Sheffer and Brad Pitt in A River Runs Through It

The program was a classic The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet because music from almost every era was on the program. A prelude and fugue by Bach started the program. Sackett has a beautiful tone, which is crystal clear, round and mellow. His interpretation seemed to be improvised. Listeners could imagine themselves listening to Bach himself seated at the organ engrossed in his thoughts and improvising as only he could. Other pieces on the program were a Sonata by Mozart, an impromptu by Schubert and representative pieces by the ragtime composer William Balcom, the Hungarian post-Romantic Erno Dohnanyi and two pieces by Chopin. As the concert progressed, I began to think that the only ingredient missing was a lack of dynamic contrast. The problem was actually with the piano, which was a bit recalcitrant in the tonal department. In reality, Xei has all of the spice needed. Despite his youth, he has a mature approach to music. Make sure to keep an eye on him. Time for dinner After the concert I was in the mood for some southern Italian food. The area near Davies Symphony Hall is loaded with restaurants and southern Italian cuisine was offered in the restaurant Doppio Zero. Its owners are from Naples and Puglia and the cuisine is representative of southern Italy. Doppio Zero is a very lively restaurant replicating the cuisine of Naples. While it is famous for pizza, I was in the mood for lasagna which was like a homemade lasagna. The atmosphere made us feel like we were eating in a fine home. Enthusiasm was everywhere. A very colorful beet salad was the perfect side dish to the lasagna. Those things should have been enough. But when you have a special dinner, you need a special dessert. A lemon sorbetto concluded the week on a very high note. Mythical elixirs are usually evasive. Always keep in mind that the good life is within reach. Education (and enthusiasm) can stave off dotage. articles.text: Troop 11 Scouts and their parents at Sugar Bowl On Friday, January 30, Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 and Troop 4 headed out from Piedmont, bound for Sugar Bowl. Scouts sang songs, played games and chatted away the time as they made their way on the highways and winding roads of Tahoe. Piling into Heidelmann Lodge, they carried their bags to the giant dormitories stocked with mattresses and fluffy pillows for all attendees from Troop 11 and Troop 4. That night the Patrols took advantage of the large well equipped kitchen. The CurlyLoos patrol had more than one pan of food cooking at once, which was a step up from the one-pan, onepot, two-burner stove setup they knew from camping in the snow and rocks of California’s beautiful national parks. The Scouts enjoyed the fruits of their labor in the warm rustic lodge, safe from the winter cold outside. They joked and laughed together, told stories and smiled. When all the dishes were done, Troop 11 was set loose. They ran through the halls, rambunctiously exploring their new home. In particular, they settled in the game room, where they played blackjack, poker, apples to apples, and hide and seek with new friends from Troop 4. Some hallways were full of excited and sweet chattering that seemed to echo off the ceilings, and others were full of the melodious music coming from very talented Scouts relishing in their luck at the inclusion of a piano among the many joys of Heidelmann Lodge. At 7 a.m. sharp the scouts woke up, ready for a new day of adventure. They pulled on thick layers and began to cook their breakfasts, which for one patrol, was cinnamon rolls, fruit and sausages. Once everything was ready to go, the Scouts enjoyed the magnificent view from the room that had hosted the majority of their merriment the night before. The windows of the game room offered a majestic scene of the mountains of Tahoe gilded in white. That morning, Troop 11 drove to Sugar Bowl thanks to parent drivers. As all good Scouts do, Troop 11 used the buddy system, so everyone skied in pairs or groups of pairs. They smoothly rocketed down the slopes, leaning this way and that, planting their poles appropriately and taking in the magical mountains and the crisp, clean air. Everyone was able to find their groove though the conditions were not perfect and many fell into the fluffy cold banks. Some Scouts tried new techniques and others tried new levels. One pair of Scouts skied down a terrain and caught two feet of air before landing on their butts. Another pair continued to explore the resort until the last lift at 4:30 p.m. They watched the sun set in the mountains as they returned to the lodge, where they relaxed and recharged from their epic day under the frosted forest and blue skies of Tahoe. They cooked more warm meals (like fried rice and spring rolls) that made their bellies and hearts sing with the joy of a dinner well enjoyed. Of course, more games and songs were played that night. They will live in these Scouts memories forever. The next morning was another early one. The Scouts packed and rushed through the motions of getting ready, bumping into each other and generally experiencing a hectic exit. But everyone made it home safely, and some took a detour to a ski resort, where they enjoyed another day on the white slopes that sparkled like jewels in the sun. Isabelle Meyers is a member of Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 11. Scouts and parents regroup on the slopes.

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays group will return to Mountain View Cemetery on April 15 for its 8th annual Spring Tour conducted by author and Mountain View docent Dennis Evanosky. This tour will be his fourth with Walking on Wednesdays. He took the group for well attended walks in April 2023, 2024, and 2025. Evanosky has written two books about Oakland’s history, Oakland’s Mountain View Cemetery and Oakland’s Laurel District. Since their first walk on April 18, 2018, the group has gone on over 360 walks. A visit to the cemetery with its beautiful spring flowers and expansive views of the Bay has become an annual memorable event. Walkers will meet in front of Mountain View’s main mausoleum. The tour will start at 10:30 a.m. and last for about 1 hour and 30 minutes. The cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue at the end of Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. There is no charge for the event, and free parking is available inside the cemetery. For more information, contact activity leader Dick Carter at camktgrp@comcast.net.

Lion with blood transfusion By Isabella Linares On Friday, March 6, Oakland Zoo helped rescue a female mountain lion cub from El Dorado County. California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW) veterinarians performed an initial comprehensive exam, noting she was severely emaciated, weighing less than half of her ideal weight, and was weak and infested with ticks. The assessment also showed gastrointestinal issues, but there were no signs of trauma. After treating her for dehydration and tick infestation, the cub was taken to Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital for further care. There, she was confirmed to be in a critically fragile state, highlighting the importance of quick rescue and intervention “Oakland Zoo has made major advances in medical care and treatment of critically ill orphaned mountain lion cubs,” said Dr. Deana Clifford, CDFW Senior Wildlife Veterinarian. “We are grateful for the continued partnership with Oakland Zoo that can give these cubs a better chance at survival.” The mountain lion cub, now named Clover, was moved to the ICU at the Oakland Zoo Veterinary Hospital and has been receiving around-the-clock intensive care from the Veterinary Hospital and Animal Care staff for the past few days. On the morning of Monday, March 9, her condition started to worsen, and Oakland Zoo Veterinary and Animal Care staff administered life-saving care, including a blood transfusion using blood from one of their resident mountain lions, Briar. Briar was rescued in August 2024 in El Dorado County and has remained a resident of the California Trail habitat at Oakland Zoo, along with fellow rescues Coloma and Silverado. “This is a journey we are always committed to undertakPhotos by Oakland Zoo Mountain lion cub Clover was brought to the Oakland Zoo Veterinary Hospital on March 6. Clover receives a blood transfusion on March 9. Clover was half her normal weight on March 6. ing. Our teams dedicate their hearts, skills, and resources to every rescue we handle. Regardless of the outcome, we remain here to assist and aim to leave a lasting positive impact on their lives,” says Dr. Lauren Pudenz, Associate Veterinarian at Oakland Zoo. Clover is the Zoo’s 32nd mountain lion cub rescue as part of the Rescue and Recovery program and a member of the Bay Area Cougar Action Team. Oakland Zoo emphasizes the importance of quickly reaching out to CDFW or permitted wildlife rehabilitators when you see injured or sick wildlife like Clover in the wild. Acting swiftly with professional help greatly increases these animals’ chances of survival. When you encounter injured or ill wildlife, it is essential to contact CDFW or a permitted rehabilitator right away, stay at a safe distance to avoid causing additional harm to yourself or the animal, and refrain from feeding or trying to rehabilitate the animal yourself. This helps prevent the spread of disease, reduces the risk of harm, and helps stop wildlife from entering human-populated areas, which can cause them to be displaced. How old is Clover? She is about three months old based on her coat coloration and tooth development. What happened to Clover’s mom? The first priority when CDFW finds a puma kitten is to assess whether the area is safe — away from roads and other dangers — and whether the kitten appears relatively healthy. If so, CDFW will leave the cub in place and monitor it with a camera to see if the mother returns. They have also attempted reunions before. They generally avoid removing a wild kitten if its mother is nearby. Unfortunately, Clover was found near a road, and given how emaciated she was, it was clear she hadn’t been cared for in some time, making her mother’s presence very unlikely. Regional staff checked reports of mountain lion appearances in the area but didn’t find any, so CDFW doesn’t know who her mother was. Residents are encouraged to report any additional sightings. How do you get a blood donor for a mountain lion? Oakland Zoo Veterinary and Animal Care staff conduct voluntary training with all animal residents to showcase different behaviors, helping staff better care for them. Briar has been participating in voluntary training to prepare for his own care, and sometimes this training can be used for life-saving procedures, like this blood transfusion for Clover. Severely emaciated animals are often anemic due to their bodies lacking enough nutrients to make red blood cells and other critical blood components. Often this is compounded by additional disease processes such as parasites or infections, which these debilitated cubs have a hard time handling. What conservation challenges do mountain lions face in the wild? Mountain lions encounter numerous conservation challenges in the wild. Their habitats are increasingly fragmented as new communities encroach, slicing through mountain lion territories and blocking essenBriar, a 2024 Mt. Lion rescue, donates blood for the mountain lion cub Clover. tial movement pathways with highways and buildings. Human expansion increases the risk of fatal car strikes; when a mother mountain lion is hit, her cubs often cannot survive without her for food and guidance. Additionally, like many other wild animals in California, mountain lions are threatened by wildfires driven by climate change. Will Clover be released to the wild? In the wild, mountain lion cubs need about two years with their mother to learn survival skills. Because Clover is so young, she lacks those skills and cannot be released back into the wild. What is the Bay Area Cougar Action Team (BACAT)? In 2012, the Oakland Zoo participated in a training session focused on resolving conflicts between humans and wildlife. This training led to the formation of BACAT. The alliance brings together various agencies, nonprofit organizations, local parks, and mountain lion researchers. With a shared message and a team-based approach, BACAT aims to create a support system that serves as a model for other regions in California and beyond. Through BACAT, Oakland Zoo has rescued and rehabilitated over 30 mountain lions, most of whom were victims of human-wildlife conflicts or wildfires. How much does it cost Oakland Zoo to care for mountain lion cubs? Cubs come to Oakland Zoo with varying medical needs and symptoms; some stay only a matter of weeks, while others may stay for many months. On average, mountain lion cubs spend 8.5 days in the Intensive Care Unit at the Wayne and Gladys Valley Veterinary Hospital, which requires constant staff care. The average cub costs roughly $18,000 per month for veterinary and animal care. These efforts are supported by community donations. How can you help support Oakland Zoo’s Mountain Lion Rescue program Oakland Zoo relies on community philanthropic support to fund our conservation and animal welfare programs, including our mountain lion rescue and recovery work. You can make a donation to Oakland Zoo online at www.oaklandzoo.org/give or reach our Development team at impact@oaklandzoo.org. Isabella Linares is with Oakland Zoo. articles.text: and Debbi DiMaggio At the heart of ‘April in Paris’ is a mission that matters: supporting extraordinary care at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland. Please join us on April 11 at the Claremont Country Club for a memorable evening of mingling, music, and dancing, all in support of children and families who rely on this exceptional hospital. Through its fundraising efforts, Hill Branch helps ensure that every child can receive the care they need, regardless of background, circumstance, or a family’s ability to pay. Buy your tickets today and help make extraordinary care possible for more children and families. HillBranch.org. The grateful parent letter that follows is a moving reminder of the very real difference this care makes. It speaks to the compassion, expertise, and hope families find at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland during their most difficult moments. On November 3, 2025, our family’s life changed forever when what should have been A routine 6-year-old checkup turned into every parent’s worst nightmare. I will forever be grateful to Dr Courtney Pickering, who completed her pediatric residency at the University of California, San Francisco, and is now my daughter’s primary pediatrician. During Hailey’s checkup, she noticed that Hailey’s coloring was just slightly off and sent us to UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland for blood work. Just as we were driving home from the hospital, we received a call from Dr. Pickering, who told us to go home, pack a bag, and return to the hospital immediately. My Hailey is receiving great care at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital. heart sank. When we arrived at the ER, the team was already expecting us. Not all of the blood work had come back yet, but even from the basic panel, it was clear that Something was very wrong. Minutes felt like days as I sat holding my baby girl in disbelief, still not knowing the underlying cause. Everything from that moment forward feels like a blur. I remember Hailey being scared, and a nurse going to the annex to find a very special elephant hospital gown just for her. The standard gowns for children her age are cheerful with teddy bear prints, but this one was one of a kind—and it instantly made Hailey feel special. Hailey has never been just a number there. Even though families travel from near and far for the care provided at UCSF Benioff, every child is treated with compassion, dignity, and love. We were admitted to a room on the fifth floor while we waited for more answers. I didn’t know it at the time, but that room would become my home for the next 14 days. The doctors explained that they were still waiting on additional tests, but it was likely leukemia. In the meantime, Hailey received three blood transfusions. Eventually, the words no parent is ever prepared to hear became our reality. Hailey was diagnosed with B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL), the most common childhood cancer. We know that in 50 years it’s probably going to be warmer than we are right now,” said Kent. Piedmont is working with Devil Mountain, a wholesale nursery specializing in growing trees for a changing climate. The nursery is planting trees native to Southern California or Mexico that are more adaptable to the temperatures Piedmont is now facing. The city is planting Quercus Tomentella, an island oak tree native to Channel Islands of California and Guadalupe Island. “It (Island Oak) is very drought-tolerant and will be more NOTICE TO CONTRACTORS adaptive than our California coast live oak. This might be one of the alternatives in the oak species that will be a good replacement, because it’ll be happier in the drier climate,” said Kent. Planting an oak is extra special because it helps stimulate the local environment. Kent cited Doug Tallamy, an entomologist and author who highlights oaks as the single most critical plant genus for supporting wildlife, biodiversity, and ecosystem health in North America. “Oaks support more bees and bugs than any other species. So there’s something about planting an oak tree that is really beneficial for the native habitat,” she explained. Plant a tree; help your community As the city continues to plant trees more adaptive to the changing climate, residents can support this initiative by contacting the city to plant a street tree in front of their home. The city will plant the tree, stake it, and give the resident a watering bag. The city requests that residents water the tree weekly for the first year to help the tree become established. If you are interested in planting a street tree in front of your home residents can call (510) 420-3064 or email nkent@piedmont.ca.gov.
